claim:
\begin{abstract}
Many machine-learning tasks, including representation learning, rely on
negative examples that are constructed rather than directly observed. This
issue is especially important for protein--protein interaction (PPI)
prediction, where experimentally established non-interactions are scarce. PPI models are therefore commonly trained and evaluated against sampled, unobserved protein pairs
treated as negatives. We study how this construction affects model
comparison. Keeping positives, protein-disjoint splits, class balance, and
model selection fixed, we vary training and evaluation negatives
independently across six constructions and four sequence-based models, three
of which use protein language model (pLM) representations. Changing only the
test negatives shifts AUPRC by up to 0.26, and the top-ranked architecture
changes with the construction. Negatives matched to true partners in pLM
representation space reduce the evaluated pLM-based models to near-chance
performance in this constructed setting. We correct an identifier-lookup error
that invalidated the submitted partner-shuffling conclusion; the corrected
results show dependence on original pairs in some settings. Absolute AUROC on
measured assay outcomes is often close to chance. A new 1024-residue experiment
retains more training positives and confirms sensitivity to negative construction,
although individual model results vary. A fully random-pair training control
also shows architecture-dependent effects. We document the evaluation pipeline
and distinguish verified private results from artifacts not yet approved for release. Our results
show that with constructed negatives, model comparisons are not just noisy
but systematically sensitive to how negatives are defined, a methodological
choice that is often left implicit.
\end{abstract}

construction. Anchor-based negatives matched in ESM-2 space are challenging

interactome prediction \citep{zhang2025humanppi}, and the graph-level PRING

claim:
\paragraph{Dataset shortcuts.}
Distribution shift and leakage remain central issues in protein ML. FLIP2
explicitly evaluates protein models under application-relevant distribution
shifts \citep{didi2026flip2}; PRING introduces redundancy- and
leakage-controlled PPI network evaluation \citep{zheng2025pring}; and
\citet{bernett2024} showed that protein sharing, sequence similarity, and
interacting hubs can strongly affect sequence-based PPI evaluation. DataSAIL
provides a general similarity-aware splitting framework
\citep{joeres2025,joeres2026addendum}. Pretrained representations create a
separate exposure issue because downstream benchmark proteins or close relatives
may occur in the pretraining corpus \citep{szymborski2026}. Taxonomic identity
can also be recoverable from protein representations \citep{hallee2026}; our
main Gold experiment is human-only, so we do not interpret taxonomy as a
Gold-specific shortcut.

\paragraph{Uniform.} A replacement partner is sampled uniformly from the
stage-specific candidate set. Uniform sampling does not match
per-protein properties between classes and therefore leaves protein-level
shortcuts available.
\paragraph{Degree-matched.} The replacement partner minimizes the absolute
difference from the train-visible network degree of the observed positive
partner. On the protein-disjoint Gold test set, train-visible degree is
degenerate because test proteins are absent from the training network, so this
test construction is retained as a diagnostic condition.
\paragraph{Sequence-matched.} Each protein is represented by
$\log(1+\mathrm{length})$ and the frequencies of the 20 standard amino acids,
standardized within the split; the allowed replacement partner minimizing
Euclidean distance to the observed partner is selected.
\paragraph{ESM-matched.} The same fixed-anchor rule is applied in cached
single-protein ESM-2 (150M) representation space, using final-layer
overlap-corrected mean-pooled 640-dimensional vectors
\citep{lin2023esm2}. The representation cache is fixed before PPI training.
Because three evaluated architectures share the ESM2 encoder family, this
negative construction is a representation-coupled stress test, not a set of
verified non-interactions. In the 1024-residue test it yields 996 repeated
negative rows versus 129 for Uniform and uses its most common replacement
protein 172 times versus 22.
\paragraph{Bernett-ILP.} We implement the global ILP negative construction of
\citet{bernett2026} on the fixed candidate-pair set, with equal weights on
degree, taxon-pair counts, self-interactions, and mean Gene Ontology Biological
Process Jaccard discrepancy.
\paragraph{TPPNI-balanced.} We reproduce the degree-constrained
configuration-model and Contrastive-L3 candidate generation of
\citet{chatterjee2025}, then take a predefined deterministic 1:1 subset.

\paragraph{Different negative constructions leave different shortcuts
available.}
Reducing one shortcut does not remove all simple predictive signals. The
original easy-property and single-protein controls remain in Appendix
Figure~\ref{fig:supp-shortcut-controls}. A particularly informative baseline
uses a logistic classifier on the sum and absolute difference of pooled ESM-2
protein embeddings. On the 1024-residue Gold Uniform/Uniform setting, this
classifier reaches AUROC 0.643 (AUPRC 0.641), compared with AUROC 0.691 for
Frozen-ESM2, 0.723 for TUnA, 0.581 for D-SCRIPT, and 0.525 for RAPPPID
(Fig.~\ref{fig:baseline-comparison}). The pooled logistic classifier exceeds
D-SCRIPT and RAPPPID on all six matched training/test constructions, but not
Frozen-ESM2 or TUnA. Because the absolute-difference feature depends on
both proteins, it is not strictly protein-only. A separate sum-only additive
logistic control reaches AUROC 0.570 on Uniform/Uniform. These controls expose
